body:
A new concrete driveway costs $6 to $15 per sq ft installed in 2026, with a plain two-car driveway at $2,400 to $8,600 in HomeGuide data. Angi data in the same guides puts many driveways at $8 to $20 per sq ft, with an average total near $6,400. Your size, thickness, finish, and site work decide where your quote lands in that range.

## The 2026 cost table by size and finish

HomeGuide lists a concrete driveway at $6 to $15 per sq ft on average for materials and labor. The low end is a plain gray slab with a broom finish on a flat site. The high end covers thicker pours, color, borders, and harder access.

| Driveway size | Square feet | Low at $6 per sq ft | Typical at $10 per sq ft | High at $15 per sq ft |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 12 x 24 ft, one car | 288 | $1,728 | $2,880 | $4,320 |
| 20 x 20 ft | 400 | $2,400 | $4,000 | $6,000 |
| 24 x 24 ft, two car | 576 | $3,456 | $5,760 | $8,640 |
| 24 x 36 ft, three car | 864 | $5,184 | $8,640 | $12,960 |

Finish changes the rate a lot. HomeGuide breaks a concrete driveway into tiers: standard plain concrete at $6 to $10 per sq ft, basic decorative work at $10 to $15, mid-range stamped work at $15 to $20, and high-end custom work at $20 to $25 or more per sq ft. A stamped pattern that looks like stone costs far more than a plain slab, even at the same size and thickness.

| Cost item | DIY cost | Pro cost | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete and base, plain slab | Material only, about half the pro total | $6 to $15 per sq ft installed | Pro price covers forms, pour, finish, and joints |
| Old driveway removal | Dump fees plus tool rental | $2 to $6 per sq ft | Reinforced concrete costs more to break and haul |
| Rebar upgrade | Material only | $1 to $3 per sq ft | Helps on soft soil and for heavy vehicles |
| Sealing after cure | Material only | $1 to $3 per sq ft | Optional for plain concrete, advised for decorative work |

DIY on a full driveway saves labor but holds real risk. You still pay for concrete, gravel, forms, mesh or rebar, tool rental, and dump fees. If the finish goes wrong or the slab drains to the garage, removal costs more than the labor you saved.

## Worked example: a 24 x 24 ft two-car driveway

Take a standard two-car driveway, 24 x 24 ft (7.3 x 7.3 m), poured 4 in thick on a gravel base, plain broom finish, no old driveway to remove.

Step 1, area. 24 ft x 24 ft = 576 sq ft.

Step 2, price range. Low: 576 x $6 = $3,456. Typical: 576 x $10 = $5,760. High: 576 x $15 = $8,640. That matches the HomeGuide two-car range of $2,400 to $8,600 in the rate table, with our high end a few dollars over due to rounding the rate to $15.

Step 3, concrete volume, checked for the order. Volume in cubic feet = 576 sq ft x 4 in / 12 = 192 cu ft. Cubic yards = 192 / 27 = 7.11 cu yd. Add 10 percent for waste and an uneven base: 7.11 x 1.10 = 7.82 cu yd. Rounded up like a buyer, you order 8 cu yd of ready-mix.

Step 4, check the volume a second way. One cubic yard at 4 in thick covers 81 sq ft. 576 / 81 = 7.11 cu yd, which matches Step 3. With the 10 percent extra, the order is still 8 cu yd rounded up.

Step 5, check the price a second way. At the typical $10 rate, 100 sq ft costs $1,000. The driveway has 5.76 units of 100 sq ft, so 5.76 x $1,000 = $5,760, which matches Step 2.

If you need old asphalt or concrete removed first, add $2 to $6 per sq ft. On 576 sq ft that is $1,152 to $3,456 on top of the new pour. Get that as a separate line, not buried in the per foot rate. To check slab volume for any size, use our [concrete calculator](/blog/concrete-calculator/).

## What pushes the price up or down?

Thickness is the quiet cost driver. A 4 in slab is standard for cars. A 5 or 6 in slab, or a thickened edge, uses more concrete and more base. HomeGuide notes a 4 in slab at a lower installed rate than a 6 in slab. If you park an RV, a work truck, or a dumpster on the drive, pay for the thicker pour and rebar now. A cracked thin slab costs more to replace than the extra inch cost on day one.

Site work comes next. Grading runs about $3 to $8 per sq ft in the HomeGuide driveway data summaries, or $700 to $2,500 for many lots. A drain to move water away from the garage can add $1,000 to $4,000. Tight access that needs a pump truck, a long wheelbarrow run, or hand work also adds labor.

Finish and detail add up fast. Color in the mix, a stamped pattern, a contrasting border, exposed aggregate, and extra control joints all raise the rate. So do permits, at $50 to $200 in many towns for a home driveway, plus a second permit in some cities for work on the curb cut or the street apron. Ask who pulls the permit and who calls for the inspection.

Region and season matter too. Labor is the larger half of many bids, at about $3 to $5 per sq ft for slab work in HomeGuide data. Big city labor and winter work with blankets and heat cost more than a spring pour in a low cost area. Small jobs under 200 sq ft often cost more per sq ft due to minimum truck and crew fees.

## How to get a fair quote and keep the slab sound

Get three written bids on the same spec. Write the spec down: size, thickness, base depth, mesh or rebar, concrete strength, finish, joint spacing, and who removes the old surface and the spoil. A low bid that leaves out base depth or steel is not the same job as a full bid.

Ask these points on each bid. How deep is the gravel base, and will you compact it in layers? Where will water drain, and what slope will you pour, at least 1/4 in per ft away from the garage in most cases? How soon will you cut control joints? Will you keep cars off for at least 7 days? A good crew answers in plain numbers.

Hold back a final payment until the slab has cured and you have walked it after a hose test. Puddles that sit by the garage door, a joint that was never cut, and a rough patch by the apron are all easier to fix before final payment. Never pay the full price in cash before the pour.

Plan the work around cure time. You can walk on new concrete in 24 to 48 hours, but keep cars off for at least 7 days and heavy trucks off longer. Full cure takes about 28 days. Keep the surface damp in the first week in hot weather if your crew advises it, and keep de-icer off the slab in its first winter.

For a small pad or a repair, bags can make sense. For a full driveway, ready-mix is the sane route. Our [post hole concrete calculator](/blog/post-hole-concrete-calculator/) covers the bag math for posts, and the [square footage calculator](/blog/square-footage-calculator/) helps if your drive flares or has a turn-around area.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much does a 24 x 24 ft concrete driveway cost in 2026?
At $6 to $15 per sq ft installed, a 576 sq ft driveway costs $3,456 to $8,640, with a typical plain job near $5,760 at $10 per sq ft. Removal of an old drive adds $2 to $6 per sq ft.

### How thick should a concrete driveway be?
Four inches is the standard for cars on a good base. Go to 5 or 6 in for heavy trucks, an RV pad, or soft soil, and add rebar. The extra concrete costs less than a cracked slab repair.

### How long does a concrete driveway last?
HomeGuide lists a concrete driveway life of 30 to 40 years. Good base work, drainage, and joint cuts are what let a slab reach that range.

### Can I pour a driveway myself to save money?
You can, but a full driveway is a fast, heavy pour with no second chance on the finish. Most owners hire a crew for the pour and save money on clear-out, landscaping, and sealing instead. A small apron or pad is a safer DIY size.

### How much concrete do I need for a 24 x 24 ft driveway?
At 4 in thick you need 7.11 cu yd before waste. Add 10 percent and round up, so order 8 cu yd. Check any size in the concrete calculator before you call the plant.

### Do I need a permit for a new driveway?
In many towns, yes, at $50 to $200, and work on the street apron can need a city permit too. Your contractor should name the permit in the bid. Check with your town if the bid is silent on permits.
